title: Sail membranes for optomechanical accelerometry
authors: Atkin D. Hyatt, Mitul Dey Chowdhury, Mahir Chowdhury, Mohamed J. Ahamed, Dalziel J. Wilson
abstract: Strained membrane resonators have emerged as a promising platform for optomechanical accelerometry; however, the desired combination of low frequency and high $Q$-mass product requires a rethinking of their dissipation dilution engineering. Applying Bayesian optimization to a Si$_3$N$_4$ membrane, we discover a class of sail-like trampoline resonators in which the frequency is decreased by an order of magnitude while preserving the $Q$-mass product. We demonstrate centimeter-scale sails with kHz frequencies, $Q\sim10^7$ and $Q\times\text{mass}\sim$ 10 g. Vertically integrating a 7 kHz device with a nanoribbon, we realize a monolithic cavity optomechanical accelerometer with a room temperature thermal noise of $40\;\text{n}g_0/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$, sufficient to resolve $μg_0/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$ ambient vibration over a bandwidth of 4 kHz with a displacement imprecision of $10^{-14}\;\text{m}/\sqrt{\text{Hz}}$. Cryogenic arrays of sail membranes may be attractive for new physics searches and distributed quantum sensing experiments.
summary: This paper details the design and characterization of novel 'sail-like' $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$ membranes for use in ultra-sensitive optomechanical accelerometers. By employing Bayesian optimization, the authors engineered resonators that significantly boost the quality factor times mass product while lowering the resonance frequency. The resulting monolithic device demonstrates sensitivity capable of resolving microgravity accelerations, advancing fundamental physics sensing capabilities.
main_problem: The primary goal is developing highly sensitive optomechanical accelerometers by engineering strained membrane resonators to achieve a superior combination of low resonance frequency and high Q-mass product.
main_result: The authors designed 'sail-like' $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$ membranes that significantly increase the $Q 	imes m$ product while lowering the fundamental frequency, achieving sensitivities sufficient to resolve microgravity accelerations.
method: The study combines theoretical modeling (deriving noise equations based on geometry and stress) with computational optimization using Bayesian methods to guide the design of optimal membrane geometries.
model_or_system: The physical system is a strained $	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$ membrane resonator, optimized into a sail-like shape. The final device integrates this sail onto a nanoribbon acting as an inertial reference plane for monolithic cavity optomechanical sensing.
key_observables: Thermal acceleration noise ($S_{	ext{th}}^a$), resonance frequency ($f$), Quality factor ($Q$), and displacement/acceleration imprecision ($	ext{S}_{	ext{imp}x}, 	ext{S}_{	ext{imp}a}$).
important_parameters: Room temperature thermal noise of $40\;	ext{n}g_0/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$; achieving $\mu	ext{g}_0/\sqrt{	ext{Hz}}$ resolution over a 4 kHz bandwidth.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on modeling the mechanical response using continuum mechanics equations and assumes that thermal noise is the limiting factor, although discrepancies with measured Q-factors were noted.
figures_summary: Figures compare $Q 	imes m$ vs frequency for different membrane types, detail the Bayesian optimization process used to find optimal parameters, and show experimental characterization of resonance frequencies and quality factors.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from identifying the need for improved resonator design (low $f$, high $Qm$) to applying Bayesian optimization on sail geometries. It then presents measurements on optimized single sails and finally demonstrates a monolithic double-membrane setup for acceleration sensing.
why_interesting: This work is highly relevant as it pushes the boundaries of mechanical sensing by combining advanced materials science ($	ext{Si}_3	ext{N}_4$), optimization theory (Bayesian methods), and quantum/optomechanical measurement techniques to reach fundamental force detection limits.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. (a) Photo of optimized circular-fillet sail membrane with 2.5×2.5 mm2 pad and 10-µm-wide tethers. (b) Simulated von Mises stress near the tether clamps. (c) Compilation of Q × m versus fre- quency for trampoline [10, 22–24], square [25–29], phononic crystal [8, 9, 30–32], hierarchical [33], perimeter mode [34], and torsion rib- bon [35, 36] type Si3N4 membranes. Open and solid red circles are simulated and characterized sail membranes described in Figs. 2-3.

FIG. 2. Optimizing the Qm/f of a Si3N4 trampoline resonator with fixed tether width. (a) Sail-like trampoline geometries with pad-width W, tether width t, pad fillet radius R, and clamp fillet radius r. Top: square-fillet sail (W independent of R). Bottom: circular-fillet sail (W = R). (b-c) Sweep of W over optimized fillets (yellow markers) with t = 10 µm. Plots show quality factor Q, frequency f, maximum von Mises stress, effective mass m, and Qm/f versus W. (d-e) Bayesian optimization algorithm convergence (d) and design objective landscape (e) for the bottom device in (a). Colored points in (d) correspond to the same points in (e).

FIG. 3. Device characterization. (a) Energy ringdown of three sail membranes with the geometry shown in Fig. 1a. Exponential fits yield quality factors as high as Q = 10 × 106. (b) Free-running vi- bration spectra (blue) showing the 7 kHz fundamental membrane mode. Overlaid is the driven response of the 200-µm-thick device chip (brown) and a similar 400-µm-thick chip (light brown) taken with a scanning vibrometer at atmospheric pressure, showing broad resonances at 12 and 25 kHz, respectively. Insets: simulated mem- brane modeshapes and measured chip modeshapes.

FIG. 4. Dual membrane accelerometry with an optimized circular-fillet sail membrane as a test mass and a ribbon membrane as a reference surface. (a) Image of sail-on-ribbon device released from a 200-µm-thick Si substrate. The top membrane has the sail geometry shown in Fig. 1a. The bottom membrane is a 200-µm-wide ribbon [35]. (b) Transmission versus incident wavelength of double-membrane cavity with finesse ∼2. The red point indicates the maximum fringe slope and operating wavelength. (c-e) Free-running displacement (c) and acceleration (d,e) spectra measured with power ¯P = {5,50,500,1000} µW. Insets show scaling of noise floor and thermal noise bandwidth versus ¯P.
